OpenAI's AI tunes AMD chips

18 November 2026 · Reading time: 5 minutes

OpenAI says its models improved power, performance and area on AMD's flagship GPU design by up to 14 percent, and some of the changes are already in a chip AMD sent for manufacturing.

Sapaude retells the story in its own words. The source is below. Publisher: Sapaude.

In three points

Three points, in this order: what the source shows, where that claim stops, and what to check next.

  1. On November 18, OpenAI said its models rewrote parts of the SystemVerilog RTL for AMD's flagship GPU IP and reached up to 14 percent better power, performance and area (PPA) against what it calls heavily optimized baselines.
  2. The figure comes from OpenAI. It is a best case, not split across the three measures, and no AMD product is named. A design sent for manufacturing is not yet a measured chip; only OpenAI's own Jalapeño results are described as silicon proven.
  3. OpenAI also reports single-digit gains on key blocks of AMD's next flagship CPU, RISC-V tests across model generations, and a new model, GPT-Synopsys, built with the chip-software maker Synopsys.

Rewritten code inside AMD's GPU design

On November 18, 2026, OpenAI published a report on how its models are being used in chip design. The central claim concerns AMD. OpenAI says it worked with the chipmaker on its flagship GPU IP, the reusable design behind AMD's top graphics chip, and saw improvements of up to 14 percent in power, performance and area against heavily optimized baselines. Chip teams call that trio PPA.

The model got there by rewriting SystemVerilog RTL, the code that describes a chip's circuits. OpenAI describes the result as roughly a year of progress in less than five months. According to the post, AMD has already included some of the changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing and added others to its production design files for future versions. AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains across key blocks of its upcoming flagship CPU, using designs written by OpenAI's model.

Checked by the tools chip teams already use

OpenAI says the model reasons about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect and can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations or move data. Every rewrite went through Synopsys tools, standard software for designing and verifying chips. They checked that the block still behaved the same and scored the trade-off between power, performance and area.

The approach started with Jalapeño, OpenAI's first custom inference chip, which the company first described in August. Engineers began using GPT-o3 mini on it in early 2025. In the matrix unit, one multiplier redesign used about 15 percent less cell area in synthesis and cut latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign saved about 15 percent area at the same two-cycle latency. Across the design, OpenAI's team estimates that model-proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13 percent in the vector unit and 10 percent in the matrix unit. Those optimizations were silicon proven when the first Jalapeño chips were brought up.

To compare model generations, OpenAI also tested two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores, PicoRV32 and Ibex. At a budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT-6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both, when improving the existing design and when designing a core from written requirements. The evaluation covered 9,881 scored runs.

One best case, reported by one side

The 14 percent is OpenAI's number. The post does not break it down into power, performance and area, does not say which blocks it applies to and does not name the AMD product. "Up to" marks a maximum, not an average. The AMD results appear in OpenAI's post; it contains no separate breakdown from AMD.

There is also a gap between stages. A design sent for manufacturing is not yet a measured chip. OpenAI describes only the Jalapeño work as proven in silicon. The company names a limit of its RISC-V results itself: when designing from requirements, models could leave out features of the original cores, such as performance counters and extra instructions, which may explain part of their higher scores. Stricter area limits and timing checks after physical synthesis would make the test closer to production chip design, OpenAI writes.

Synopsys gets its own model

OpenAI is now partnering with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsys, a model meant to use Synopsys design tools the way expert chip designers do. The company expects further gains on GPU and CPU designs on top of the most optimized baselines.

For the AI industry, the loop is the point: models are being used to improve the hardware the next models will run on. Whether the 14 percent holds up will show once AMD ships the chips and independent measurements exist.

What you can do

AI is starting to work on the chips that run AI. The 14 percent is OpenAI's best case on design files; measurements from finished AMD chips do not exist yet.
